rules.statement: Endpoints and services get the per-request OpenID context from the feature published on the HttpContext (`HttpContext.GetOpenIdContext()`) and never build an `OpenIdContext` themselves.
rules.why: Endpoint filters build the context once per request and publish it, so a new endpoint needs no context plumbing and every surface stays on the same flow. The ADR calls an endpoint that builds its own context a smell.
rules.check: Look for endpoint or service code that calls the context factory or constructs an `OpenIdContext` directly instead of reading it from the HttpContext feature.

rules.statement: When an operation acts on a tenant other than the one the request's context carries, such as a management route naming a tenant or a background job, materialize that tenant's own context explicitly instead of reusing the request's context.
rules.why: The request's context carries the host's tenant. Reusing it would key grants, sign logout tokens and audit in the wrong tenant's security domain.
rules.check: In a management handler or background job that takes a tenant id, check whether tenant-bound services (sessions, grants, logout, signing) run on the ambient request context instead of a context created for the addressed tenant.

rules.statement: A context materialized explicitly for an addressed tenant is owned by the caller: dispose it, and never publish it as the request's context feature.
rules.why: Only the request and control-plane paths publish on the request. Explicit and background contexts are disposable and owned by whoever created them.
rules.check: Look for `CreateForTenantAsync`/`CreateForBackgroundAsync` results that aren't disposed (no `using`), or that get set as the HttpContext's context feature.

rules.statement: Materializing a tenant by explicit id loads it fresh from the tenant store under its own stored issuer, and must not seed the tenant or read or write the tenant cache.
rules.why: An administrative operation must act on the tenant as stored at that moment. The ADR calls a cache read or write on the explicit path a smell.
rules.check: In the by-id or explicit tenant materialization path, look for tenant-cache lookups or inserts, or a call into seeding or provisioning.

rules.statement: A missing or disabled tenant, or a tenant whose team is disabled, answers 404 before it is seeded or cached, so a disabled tenant is never put in the tenant cache.
rules.why: Resolution on the load path is the authoritative validation. Cache hits are deliberately not re-validated, so nothing invalid may enter the cache.
rules.check: In tenant resolution or caching code, check that the disabled and missing checks (tenant and team) run before seeding and before the cache insert.

rules.statement: A tenant strategy's `TryGetTenantId` probe must be store-free and non-throwing: it returns the identifier only when the request alone determines it, and otherwise returns false.
rules.why: The warm path probes the tenant cache with this identifier so that it doesn't pay a tenant-store round-trip. A probe that reads the store or throws defeats that.
rules.check: Look for `TryGetTenantId` implementations that call a store, are async, or throw, instead of returning false when they can't know the id.

rules.statement: Make a per-tenant behavioral knob a setting on the resolved tenant that can be overridden below the platform, not a process-wide start-up option.
rules.why: Per-tenant control is data-driven, and settings merge from the platform, the team and the tenant, so both protocol and management surfaces see the effective value.
rules.check: Look for new options-class properties or start-up configuration that control behavior that should vary per tenant.

rules.statement: Register each setting descriptor exactly once: surface-neutral descriptors in the core slice, and protocol descriptors contributed by the authentication slice as an additional source.
rules.why: The setting catalog is shared, and duplicated descriptors would let the surfaces drift apart.
rules.check: Look for a setting descriptor defined or registered in more than one slice, or a protocol-specific descriptor added to the core slice.

rules.statement: Keep the session service bound to its OpenID context, and don't add tenant-parameterized overloads to it. Callers needing another tenant materialize that tenant's context instead.
rules.why: The termination seam needs a materialized tenant to sign logout tokens, so tenant overloads would collapse into a context anyway while forking the service surface.
rules.check: Look for new session-service members that take a tenant id parameter.
